notes.title: [DevLog] Dynamic Pixel Object Rendering
notes.content:
Hello!
Today, I’d like to share the process of dynamically rendering pixel art.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/4e6353a9b5c48b981bd0e4c6be2a587f731ac298.gif[/img]

The reason for implementing this at first was for a newly added monster.
It needed to smash the ground around it freely with its head, which was hard to express with simple images.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/bef858c63f7e7724f4d55cb1802ed8bf9356b0d5.gif[/img]

So I used RenderTextures to draw pixels.

The initial implementation was heavily hardcoded, and the algorithm was unstable at times.
But I wrapped it up roughly for the first attempt.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9b7d08ff923ff1e15f27d9a19730a36f989bf022.png[/img]

Later, I came up with a new monster design.
This required using dynamic rendering again, and I decided to refine it for broader applications.



[h3]New Implementation[/h3]


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/be7709b03c2b0760169b14c87ff00d87a9ea2397.gif[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/a97b246ed839d5d050afe6e987c72725885d0c40.gif[/img]

In the new method, I switched to mesh rendering.
It’s more stable in various situations.
To do this, I first implemented the ability to draw pixelated shapes onto a RenderTexture.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/18006eab60a2910e4cdf386c989068fd82ed2b35.jpg[/img]At first, I tried checking each pixel one by one. Implementation was simple but very slow.
I thought it might be due to computation cost, so I also tried ComputeShaders, but that was even slower.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/1532208c80eebb00f8e99556685a245d877d3a95.jpg[/img]
The fastest method was the scanline algorithm I found through Google.
It splits a triangle into two parts and fills pixels using slopes.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/144c253dad534e92bb08c51b25be8535202b64ad.jpg[/img]
Performance was fine, but when rendering meshes, gaps sometimes appeared.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/a01452d6cd0a7bed40190896cdbd678f0dd46207.gif[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/ef86dca7dcdbd82ec964c001a93b0dd2fb3e85d3.gif[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/18916d777af76a7f71c9a089b37a036547e5cb32.gif[/img]

I revised the algorithm until it stabilized across various cases.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/4204271e8fe079c8115904d9c8f13d4c356b856a.gif[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/3cc2e69eb49aa6125718964b65b985048d9eba18.gif[/img]

Finally, I reached a stable version.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/fd4e959bc1dfede6631b5922b835bdebba29b4cb.gif[/img]

Here is the completed monster.



[h3]Various Applications[/h3]

Thanks to modularization, I was able to apply it to other systems as well.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/721c4b7703ce3292eccf33a120c29b502763baee.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/2def7f1f5e44c6e07fcde787d241bed2df7a32ca.png[/img]

Shadowmap and background mapping calculations in the editor became faster.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/c1aa31563b1640052f473881b6190e34e08291d9.gif[/img]

The burning effect in the game was also replaced with the new module, improving performance.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/77ea6d623a74cc85dfa889d91d63313658406d8e.gif[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/523f290e444b4f0daea6f6ac251f28ff219620b9.gif[/img]

Finally, I was also able to create a pixel rope effect based on the new module.


Thank you for reading!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9034c6554a10b90cd16ecab46234c48422c9c42e.gif[/img]

notes.title: [DevLog] Door Improvement - Editor Edition
notes.content:
Hello!
Today, I’d like to talk about the work we did to make placing doors (and windows) easier.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/47652b120a3b1c80350caa9088276063b77211d2.png[/img]
In our previous game, placing doors was relatively difficult.
The reason it was difficult was because you had to create a hole in the wall before placing a door.



[h3]The pain of placing doors and windows[/h3]

Since our game is tile-based, holes also had to be made in tile units.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/71d1fbb5cc6e1414d0852ee8d2004bf998ead1ac.png[/img]
However, doors are not sized exactly to fit a tile.
In other words, the door image inevitably had to include graphics to fill the wall gap.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/cfa73e0e579987ee165e6af482f1d7293b8853c8.jpg[/img]
Also, to finely adjust the position of a door, we needed another version of the image with a different background.
To support placing a door offset by half a tile, we had to create both versions like above.


Still, we developed while enduring this hassle.
Game development produces mountains of issues, and unless they’re critical, we often overlook them.



[h3]The door issue that finally stood out[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/227ae47b8c176220302ee92732ca8efdfbf7b32c.jpg[/img]
Walls implemented not with tilemaps, but with mesh renderers were added to our game.
And we needed to attach doors to these walls.

While tilemaps let us make holes on a grid, meshes require more complex calculations.
We’d even need to create a tool for carving holes.
So we started looking for a simpler method.



[h3]Improvement 1[/h3]

Through some research, we found people use stencil buffers in such cases.
Stencil buffers are special rendering buffers used for masking, allowing certain areas to be rendered or not.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/e71920892b4e63c4d0bbde564025ca202c9fb7db.png[/img]
In the example above, only areas marked with 1 in the stencil buffer are rendered.
Unity's ShaderLab supports the stencil feature, so we used it to modify our door like this:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/febed460882750a48dc2bc889de16bdb9927285d.png[/img]
We used a texture for the darker area of the door, masking it with stencil so that the wall behind wouldn’t render.
The door frame was floated slightly in front of the wall to avoid z-fighting. ←!
It was a convenient method, and we used it for a while, but even this had its problems.



[h3]A new problem[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/21f6ce9773e1fc9ddc93aba282067a627594c439.png[/img]
Characters would sometimes render between the door and the wall.
It didn’t happen often—it only occurred when the Y position was aligned just right—but it was very annoying as a developer.

This happened because there was a tiny actual gap between the frame and the wall.
But if we pushed the frame closer to the wall, z-fighting would occur.



[h3]Improvement 2[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/cf3ffd206778001f711bb6f84f3c670cbf244bfa.png[/img]
So we created a new mask texture.
This mask included not just the hole but also the frame area.
In other words, we cut out the frame too.

This allowed us to place the frame flush with the wall without causing z-fighting.
But it meant needing an extra texture, which was a bit inconvenient.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/c41c50a1cb93dce6b20daf9361d3d6cfb6667634.png[/img]
Then we came up with the idea of using the frame texture itself for masking.
We painted the hole section of the frame texture with alpha 1.
It's barely visible to the eye, but since it’s not fully transparent, the hole still gets cut.



[h3]Final Result[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/f1fcd0c34270475be9b7fe55e0e1aab376814792.gif[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/5e39fa10dab8bd5412df290f5dccd61159e4e278.gif[/img]
All the hassle was resolved, and we can now place holed objects freely and conveniently.

Thanks for reading!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9034c6554a10b90cd16ecab46234c48422c9c42e.gif[/img]

notes.title: [DevLog] The Feeling of Passing Through Doors
notes.content:
Hello!

Today, I’d like to talk about how we improved the feeling of passing through doors in our game.
Actually, this was something we worked on quite a while ago.

[h3]Initial State of the Door[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/636e661af03d0fbec29ad2fc186dfaac1b224928.gif[/img]
This is the door we originally made.

How does it look?
At the time, we didn’t feel anything uncomfortable or strange about it.

We only recognized the issue by chance, when we saw the door from another game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/d80bf66b16c476804d8d0b00d3505e677852cb86.gif[/img]
This is from a game called Causality.

Compared to our game, doesn’t the door-passing feel look much smoother?
Seeing this made us realize we needed to improve our own system.


[h3]Improving the Door Transition Feel[/h3]

We made a number of fine adjustments, but the core goal was:
“When passing through a door, it should never feel like control is interrupted or the character stops.”

- The character shouldn’t stop when passing through a door.
- Minimize fade-to-black time.
- Camera should follow smoothly.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/210992ffc44cae12f0b400ce82a24197270ab864.gif[/img]
Final result

However, this section is brief because there was still more to do.



[h3]Objects Shouldn’t Hit the Door Either[/h3]

You might think this is obvious, but in the early version of our game, thrown objects would bounce off doors.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/66a2f83124201a8654ede9f7d4662dfb3ad412da.gif[/img]
Like this.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/d696351438c4d6359126b4c6ccd4b45976df3cc5.gif[/img]
Of course, this wasn’t acceptable, so we implemented a number of improvements.
The complexity came from the fact that the two doors are physically separated.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/ae847c643cf33aba04dcf6712fbbb38cf1821bf5.gif[/img]
If handled poorly, this kind of issue can occur.
Both the object and the player move, but it looks like the player passed through the object.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/2aea1df0f3e247600238a8e53c29950e3913a6a5.gif[/img]
Here is the fixed version.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/476120e1d5d2787e97dccd5663b9629898d160c7.gif[/img]
Recently, we also implemented passing through doors with large objects.



Thanks for reading!

[img]{STEAM_C_

notes.title: [DevLog] Grass Movement
notes.content:
Hello!
Today, I’d like to briefly share how we improved the movement of grass.



[h3]Initial Version[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/17267a3a07fa5e8e602b118033dbb469a528efb3.jpg[/img]
This is the grass that existed in the early stages of development.
When we placed it in the game, the static appearance looked dull, so we tried adding a wind-swaying effect.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/992d2e1600da2a0d4eb2ec22c3026ce96ee095b5.jpg[/img]
To achieve this, we pre-baked tilted versions of the grass generated via code.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/a5b61cb104a4e6f6158b472082fbbda853406920.gif[/img]
While the added movement was nice, the auto-generated visuals weren’t particularly appealing.

Hand-drawing everything was too much work, and it didn’t seem like it would be much better anyway.
Also, having to re-bake the textures every time we modified an image was a hassle.

Still, since we couldn’t come up with a better solution, and it looked much better than static images, we just stuck with it.




[h3]New Method[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/422d4e00a07116b7a5bbec559b183f4980138b6e.gif[/img]
We happened to see a scene from the game Eastward.

There was grass swaying in the wind, and even though it was rendered using mesh bending, it didn’t feel out of place at all.
Seeing this helped us break free from the idea that pixel art had to match perfectly at the pixel level.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/77df3e78a5fb6288bc0901c3b3e0fdde5a4dcbfd.gif[/img]
Here’s an example we made using a mesh-based approach.

It was implemented by passing a curve value to a vertex shader, which then calculated the position.
Despite being pixel art, the mesh bending felt surprisingly natural.




[h3]Final Result[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9e9d657417d10a4a977edb6c2c4a0c01d433d088.gif[/img]
This method allowed for much more detailed expression than the baking method, resulting in much more responsive visuals.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/991a22b97c2115468599017c236c320252cef87f.gif[/img]
This is another scene.

We no longer had to bake textures each time the image changed, and the visual quality was vastly improved — very satisfying.



Thanks for reading!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9034c6554a10b90cd16ecab46234c48422c9c42e.gif[/img]

notes.title: [DevLog] Bridge
notes.content:
Hello!
Today, I'd like to write about how we improved the bridge in our game.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/b4a985eb97d475ab46da9ac36ae22d81d90f1681.png[/img]
In our game, terrain objects like the bridge shown above appear frequently.
Although it looks simple, it was outside of the in-game tile system, so placing it required unnecessarily complex work.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/41750bf06d6ec565e7ac137ddc48b23dcad74e85.gif[/img]
Manual placement was required to position the asset properly in 3D space, and various exception cases had to be handled.


But even when the bridge had no special gimmick, it still felt good as a decorative element, so we wanted to place more bridges.


So, we decided to systematize the bridge.


[h3]1. Plan[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/6a1a7f9f49c2bf877f360e982a55bae53b779405.png[/img]
First, we sketched a concept design for the new bridge.


One thing we had in mind when drawing the concept was a game we saw long ago called Princess Blitz.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/3ed91c216bc040a6edec4de44538af0ef3a4e080.gif[/img]
It’s something we saw quite a while ago, but it sometimes popped into our heads.
We thought it would be great if the newly created bridge could move dynamically.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/e5d424184fa69ca72c5ecf93036f3c8f198829cc.png[/img]
In the image above, we lowered the bridge, and internally we thought it looked fine.


[h3]2. Resource Standardization[/h3]

We considered how to standardize the assets to easily create bridges of various shapes.
Ultimately, we composed the bridge to match the tile size with front/back handles and planks.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/7026ee6b9439dfbac434fa417cf3d1a49f5baa84.png[/img]
The original file on the left is automatically organized into the resource on the right.
The width and height of the original resource can be longer, which increases the variation of the result.


There is no rope connecting the bridge in the illustration; the reason will become clear as you continue reading.


[h3]3. Bridge Placement Tool[/h3]

The reason for improving the bridge was to make placement as easy and simple as possible.
Explaining how the tool works in writing would be too lengthy, so it’s better to show it in action!
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9b0905f34d360d241918d86e5d66c09a30120e0a.gif[/img]


Select a bridge type and drag to create the bridge.
Editing and repositioning are also easy.


[h3]4. In-Game Polishing[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/515130471ecc3a00d6c74e12f03cab404b43defb.gif[/img]
This is the initial look of the newly implemented bridge.

The plan was to tile it and simply sway it with the character’s movement, but that was a miscalculation.
The rope appeared to be broken into segments more than expected, and the shape of the bridge didn’t look natural.


So, we began the improvement work.
The intermediate steps were not recorded because we were engrossed in the process.


It’s a shame...


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/98b4e7eae5404aedcfc13ecc7a1c264c888b99ad.gif[/img]
After many modifications, this is the completed look.
We adjusted various formulas to make it feel natural and replaced the rope with a line renderer.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/e084b3b2c5aca9766312a6b460ed7537a16c03c1.gif[/img]
The new bridge now also supports cases where the start and end heights are different, making it usable in more varied levels.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/f102ba88055f98059ea456801d859310b3ab777d.gif[/img]
Additionally, it reacts to the weight of objects placed on the bridge.


Thank you for reading!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9034c6554a10b90cd16ecab46234c48422c9c42e.gif[/img]

notes.title: [DevLog] Rope
notes.content:
Hello!

Today, I'd like to talk about the process we went through to create the initial rope in our game.



[h3]What is a Rope?[/h3]

In our game, the rope is an object that players can grab and hang onto.
It is mainly used to diversify the terrain by placing it on cliff areas.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/cdba3579ace2ed25016bb9f40d14b59d64f77118.gif[/img]


The idea for the rope started as a simple decorative element.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/4b5ac353ad4f96d76be84b9a74dd288d5005cdc4.png[/img]

In the early stages of development, we created chains as decorative background elements.
After making them, we thought it would be nice if they could move physically.

So, we used the game engine’s physics features to implement realistic movement.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/56afcc6b67e9d6de4cdaff6a1ad4c2e6efa1f69a.gif[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/e235105e4921767af51376f77a989077229f19bd.gif[/img]


Later, as time passed while creating mountain terrain levels, we were pondering what to fill into the sub-route.
At that moment, the idea of a rope – resembling the chain we had made before, but one that a character could hang from – came to mind.




[h3]The Initial Rope[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/26905b4b66bd93dc1865483165ab5b47cfe06f23.gif[/img]


Since it was just a matter of adding the hanging functionality to an already created element, the implementation was finished quickly.
However, the problem was with the appearance.

Expressing it like the original chain didn’t make it feel like a rope.




[h3]The Second Rope[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/060819c28432bd2fb2b2e039f8d4efc659ad3f50.gif[/img]

This version was modified from the initial one to eliminate gaps between each part.
Can you tell the difference from the initial version?

In fact, as I was writing this post, I mistakenly thought I had created two identical gifs.
They were almost indistinguishable...




[h3]The Third Rope[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/6ff7ffc35f4cef9a741ce5272ab3fd0107c3cf1a.gif[/img]

Changing our perspective, this time we implemented it entirely using a 3D mesh.
But after making it, it turned out even worse.



[h3]The Fourth Rope[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/73d4618464d448417b1da23c0787d44b14a759e4.gif[/img]

I thought, why not simply use the game engine's line renderer?
The implementation was the simplest, yet the appearance was the best.
Thus, this version was ultimately chosen.




[h3]Levels Featuring the Rope[/h3]

Below are the levels where the rope is used.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/1d0e34e7da2389b289a55887cb2acb651dd78cd8.gif[/img]

This is the sub-route where it was first applied.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/5e27b188f6033dce8b34696c001a06b2c9c65570.gif[/img]

A level that uses continuous ropes to traverse a cliff.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/ed0b35257671ea1d925fe4fa887b9521c00f88cd.gif[/img]

A level that bypasses a blocked path using the rope.




[h3]The Most Recent Look[/h3]

The ropes shown so far reflect how they looked when they were first made.
Now, players can grab the rope to climb up and down, and a hand grabbing the rope has been added.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/fed610615e246e11cb45899492b1b57cbb04776b.gif[/img]



Thank you for reading!

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9034c6554a10b90cd16ecab46234c48422c9c42e.gif[/img]

notes.title: [DevLog] Shadow Map
notes.content:
Hello!
This time, I’d like to share the story of how we created the shadow map.


Our team consists of just two programmers, so the game tends to look visually plain.
As such, we’ve been thinking a lot about how to make the game visuals feel richer.


One of the ideas we came up with was to add shadows to the edges of tiles.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/c13e303a8ac62bb2017f962d8100ea2b60e9528c.png[/img]


The mockup we created before making it seemed promising.
So, we decided to implement a feature to automatically generate these shadows.



[h3]First Implementation[/h3]


The first method we tried was to draw a black line along the floor edges and then blur it.
We tested this idea on the floor sections first, and it looked fine initially.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/f7dfc47e2a34f7ebfeab5d50f38b2ea646b11f11.png[/img]


But when we implemented shadows for the walls and applied it to actual maps, issues emerged.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/0e7d81da99def08995565d025b19e66a657babda.png[/img]


Shadows didn’t form adequately in map corners, and they didn’t generate correctly near objects like doors that alter terrain shapes.



[h3]Improvement[/h3]


After much thought, we recalculated height values, corner information,
and devised an algorithm to divide the shadow map into units while considering elements like doors.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/06d3ab5ed6fb0ecbfda1a75ba5682ad602791ca2.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/e1de83a121c337b7b79dab1598b875e5d20070a9.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/9f28fb2e0ac84141dea0d206828d7189fe3d1f1e.png[/img]



We thought we had solved the problem, but unexpected issues arose again.
We had overlooked the moving walls in our game.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/11bd4c6108d6080313990fb674e2d0d6e5b8a298.gif[/img]


If we simply bake the shadow map, only the walls move, excluding the shadows,
which results in shadows detaching from walls.
As seen in the scene above, an unwanted shadow appears in the middle of the hallway.



[h3]Improvement 2[/h3]


To solve the issue of shadows detaching, we calculated the physical wall information of the entire tilemap,
ensuring the shadows adhere to the walls.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/b8fa2d37a8164b26110cc4f70a2c697f40643745.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/4ae70cfc9ba0e0a90134fe1dbc41f22daaf08dfb.png[/img]


After various efforts, we finally completed the implementation.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/d0a7188b29abcc35f9b5d8cae7c4e219b9645b93.gif[/img]


Now, when the walls move, the floor shadows move along with them!

After stabilizing this feature, we also created functionality
to finely customize the shadows.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/06551ddf899a422c148a60e6780d54990d0ce553.gif[/img]


It turned out that the feature could not only be used for shadows but also for adding unique effects to the map.
(Though we’re not sure where it will actually be used.)



[h3]Shadow Texture Issue[/h3]


The baked shadows were divided into tile units.
However, separating the textures increased the file size and made them harder to manage,
so we combined them into a single texture.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/f47f5a610548619196acc04166c21164b1e003ad.png[/img]


But after combining the textures, the shadows appeared broken.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/d91a530c67eb7c9dc35a9d802210a0adde495dc2.png[/img]


This issue occurred because the resolution of the combined texture was too stretched horizontally,
but we resolved it using the sprite atlas feature provided by the engine.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/fd87b15f88e3d7e3e934e67490ab143f1892369c.png[/img]


As a result of the fix, we were able to achieve clean shadows again.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/dd630f09f37d57ac8c895c8663bdaf8c6fa601a7.png[/img]



[h3]Final Comparison[/h3]


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/34df663402f434c52de2abdc406bcb584fb86312.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/6ae14e6410ac5d4c71fa8478269f9930128ecddb.png[/img]


That’s all for today’s post.

Thank you for reading!

notes.title: [DevLog] #03 Object Sorting in Top-Down View [2/2]
notes.content:
[Translated from Korean]

Hello, this is Team OOPArts, currently developing Frostory.


During the game development process, we often encounter unexpected problems. The object sorting method mentioned in a previous post was one such issue.

In this post, we will discuss how we resolved this problem.


[b]1. Issues with the Previous Method[/b]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/294d9620f0543e007c2e9c0bb6f8b4a1b672d9b7.png[/img]

The previous method had issues handling sloped terrains. While splitting terrain tiles and sorting them based on the y-axis and z-axis was effective on flat surfaces, it showed limitations in more complex terrains.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/c8624956d4312948f273ec71055159976290f870.png[/img]

In a terrain like the one above, where the player (A), monster (B), sloped terrain, and ground need to be drawn, we must decide the criteria and order for drawing these four objects.




In the old system, the order was determined based on the y-axis and z-axis. Simply put, the closer the object was to the bottom of the y-axis or the top of the z-axis, the closer it was drawn to the camera.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/81f8f99d89b353f44a27967ba4e5b43bb0e20757.png[/img]

For objects, we used the point where they touched the ground as the center point.


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/0dcddd4b6c4c63e58c5f61ef43d85c089c12abdd.png[/img]

However, due to the nature of sloped terrain, it was impossible to determine a single center point to represent it.



[b]2. Attempts and Limitations with the Previous Method[/b]


Initially, we tried to solve the problem by splitting the slope into multiple segments.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/962c5079bb8ed59425880a3ed4d569f43ecda8a9.png[/img]

By dividing the slope as shown above and assigning different y-axes, we could handle movement below the slope without much problem.




[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/8323c9b71755ba6e0e3ad062b3b9959421809654.png[/img]

However, when moving on top of the slope, situations like the one above occurred.




This was an inevitable issue in the current system, which processes tiles and objects in the same way:

- Player (A) < Monster (B)
- Slope < Player (A)
- Monster (B) < Slope

This contradictory situation made it impossible to sort them correctly.




[b]3. Seeking Solutions: Learning from Other Games[/b]


We decided to explore how other games solved this problem. One famous game that features slopes in a top-down view is [i]CrossCode[/i].


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/6b9884d8a38d17f04671f8356cc454938fbbd7d8.png[/img]





[i]CrossCode[/i] used a 3D rendering technique involving z-testing. This method places the terrain on the z-axis and records height values in the z-buffer, rendering it like a 3D game.



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/cbd119fac77bf14eacb1a87680d4d3e5ef157124.gif[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/2b72930b7e3c7c721c836b0b182d6312d9c2c0b1.gif[/img]

It’s a game I thoroughly enjoyed playing through to the end, without realizing this was a 3D rendering technique.

They seemed to have standardized image sizes and collision sizes well enough that the 3D rendering was inconspicuous.





[b]4. Solution: Adopting 3D Rendering[/b]



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/66ee53e09b9e4594d3ba1e7750463de2095fddff.gif[/img]

Switching to a 3D rendering method required a major overhaul of the levels and systems we had previously created.

However, this decision not only solved the problem but also provided an opportunity to enhance the visual quality and technical possibilities of the game.




[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/17672e492ee3077a8d2fb435498fdbe2435091fa.gif[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/f4ea8b7585dba6f57c9f27574e264b4054b78c55.gif[/img]

Looking at the game world through a 3D camera, you can see how it’s structured. This approach fundamentally resolved the sorting issues with tiles and objects.




[b]5. Additional Benefits of 3D Rendering[/b]

The transition to 3D rendering opened up various possibilities beyond merely solving the sorting issue.


[b]a) Displaying Characters Behind Walls[/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/7dd4f1e746936cee7cf76520eaa5574e96c67f5e.gif[/img]

With shaders, we can now display characters even when they are behind walls. This feature can be utilized to improve gameplay visibility when necessary.


[b]b) Improved Decal Representation[/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/563c3a11e39d3f45c434a4bfefd6b9aba703a3df.png[/img]

Decals can now naturally adhere to walls and terrain, enhancing the fine details of the game world.


[b]c) Improved Shadow Representation[/b]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/d9bf5810ad9f644956f20bbb2e79ebb381198906.gif[/img]

Previously, shadows appeared to float when not aligned with the ground, but they now adapt naturally to the terrain.



[b]Conclusion[/b]

The process of introducing 3D rendering to solve the sorting issue was long and challenging, but it allowed us to improve the game’s quality and expand its expressive possibilities.

Thank you for reading!



[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44884140/e84b604d756068053858153ef943a3a61a5f403a.gif[/img]
If you’re interested in the game after reading this, please follow us. We will continue to write more posts about the development process.
